Pseudomonas aeruginosa
•
A Gram-negative,
biofilm-forming, opportunistic
healthcare-associated pathogen
•
Particularly associated with artificial 
nails, & moist, wet environments
•
Can cause severe fever, respiratory
distress, and lead to sepsis in 
individuals - especially newborns

pages.label: Slide 6
pages.text:
Campylobacter spp.
•
Gram-negative, comma-shaped, motile, 
bacterial cause of food borne illness in the UK
•
Roughly 80% of human cases
originate from contaminated poultry,
especially undercooked chicken
•
Campylobacter jejuni causes the
vast majority of cases (around 88%)
•
Campylobacter jejuni is also responsible for Guillain-Barré 
syndrome, a neurological complication of campylobacteriosis 
infection (see the endotoxins lecture for more info on mechanisms.)

pages.label: Slide 7
pages.text:
Salmonella spp.
•
Salmonella spp. are Gram-negative,
rod-shaped, motile bacteria
•
The primary natural reservoir of 
Salmonella is the GI tract of poultry,
cattle, pigs, birds, rodents, and reptiles
•
‘British Lion Mark’ eggs mean all 
hens have been vaccinated against
Salmonella, among other requirements
•
Undercooked, imported eggs are a known source
of Salmonella spp. outbreaks in the UK

pages.label: Slide 8
pages.text:
Escherichia coli
•
Escherichia coli is a Gram-negative, rod-shaped
(bacillus) bacterium
•
There are many different pathotypes of E. coli
•
Animal droppings on food products (like eggs) can
transmit Escherichia coli
•
Cows, sheep, goats, deer, and elk carry
E. coli naturally in their intestines asymptomatically
•
E. coli can even appear in salads due to irrigation,
nearby animal activity, manure, and food handlers

pages.label: Slide 9
pages.text:
Acinetobacter baumanii
•
Gram-negative, rod-shaped, aerobic, non-motile
bacterium
•
Primarily found in healthcare and hospital 
environments (nosocomial infection)
•
Thrives on hard surfaces, medical equipment
(catheters, ventilators, intravenous lines), 
and even sinks 
•
Outbreaks are unfortunately common in
intensive care units (ICUs) and wards with
immunocompromised patients

pages.label: Slide 10
pages.text:
Mycobacterium tuberculosis
•
The causative agent of tuberculosis (TB), an
infection primarily of the lungs
•
Has a very waxy cell wall, rich in 
mycolic acids
•
Humans are the primary natural reservoir
for the bacteria
•
TB is one of the leading causes of death
by infectious disease globally
•
India, Pakistan, Romania, Somalia, and Eritrea are the top countries of 
origin for non-UK-born TB cases (UKHSA, 2025)
M. tuberculosis in a sputum 
sample

pages.label: Slide 11
pages.text:
Treponema pallidum (syphilis)
•
Treponema pallidum is a species of Gram-negative, 
spiral-shaped, highly motile bacterium which causes the 
disease: syphilis
•
 The disease has up to four stages
•
 The bacterium is notoriously difficult
to culture, and requires co-cultivation
with Sf1Ep rabbit epithelial cells
•
Syphilis is generally easily treatable 
with penicillin G

pages.label: Slide 12
pages.text:
Syphilis – Primary Stage (1)
• Usually appears around ten days 
to three-months after first 
infection
• Usually characterised by a single, 
small, painless sore or ulcer
• Swollen lymph glands may also
accompany this

pages.label: Slide 13
pages.text:
Syphilis – Secondary Stage (2)
• A non-itchy rash may appear on the
palms of the hand and/or soles of the feet
• Swollen lymph glands may accompany 
this
• Flu-like symptoms may appear
• May present with fatigue, fever, 
patchy hair-loss, lesions, 
sore throat, and muscle aches 
Hughes (2020) BMJ Case 
Whiting (2023) American 
Journal
of Clinical Dermatology

pages.label: Slide 14
pages.text:
Syphilis – Latent Stage (3)
•
The latent stage is the ‘hidden’, asymptomatic stage of syphilis 
following the secondary stage
•
The latent stage can last for years and 
even decades
•
There are no visible signs or symptoms 
•
Diagnosed through serological testing, confirmed 
with Fluorescent Treponemal Antibody
Absorption (FTA-ABS) or Treponema pallidum
particle agglutination assay (TPPA)
Dark-field microscopy 
rapid
diagnostic test for 
syphilis

pages.label: Slide 15
pages.text:
Syphilis – Late Stage (4)
• Occurs around 10 – 30 years after 
first becoming infected with syphilis 
• This stage is extremely serious, 
resulting in severe damage to the
brain, heart, nerves, and other
organs
• The syphilis is usually 
non-contagious at this stage

pages.label: Slide 16
pages.text:
Haemophilus ducreyi (chancroid)
•
Chancroid is caused by Haemophilus
ducreyi, a Gram-negative, non-motile,
rod-shaped species of bacterium
•
Unlike syphilis, chancroid usually
presents as multiple, extremely 
painful sores, and has a shorter
incubation period of 1 – 14 days
•
Haemophilus ducreyi is more common
in lower-income nations, particularly
in sub-Saharan Africa (e.g., Malawi)

pages.label: Slide 17
pages.text:
Klebsiella granulomatis (donovanosis)
• Klebsiella granulomatis is a species of
Gram-negative, non-motile, encapsulated
rod-shaped bacterium
• May cause significant damage to the
skin and deeper tissue layers
• Treated with azithromycin or doxycycline
• Confirmed by observing ‘Donovan bodies’
in tissue samples under the microscope 
Example of Donovan body

pages.label: Slide 18
pages.text:
Ureaplasma spp. (ureaplasmosis)
•
Bacteria of the Ureaplasma genus are also able to cause urethritis.
They have no cell wall.
•
They may cause painful urination, unusual discharge, pain in the 
pelvis, and itching
•
It can cause infertility in both men 
and women
•
Can be carried as part of the normal 
microbiome, where overgrowth is 
associated with disease symptoms

pages.label: Slide 19
pages.text:
Mycoplasma genitalium (Mgen)
•
Mycoplasma genitalium is another species of bacterium,
devoid of a cell wall, capable of causing a range of 
symptoms (urethritis, proctitis, etc.)
•
Characterised by unusual discharge, pain 
during sex, pain in the lower abdomen, 
bleeding after sexual intercourse, and
burning when urinating
•
Usually treated with doxycycline 
and azithromycin

pages.label: Slide 20
pages.text:
Neisseria meningitidis (urethritis & proctitis)
•
Neisseria meningitidis is a Gram-negative, aerobic, 
non-motile, bean-shaped, diplococcus-arranged 
bacterium
•
While usually associated with meningitis, it is now 
known to also be an emerging sexually 
transmissible bacterium
•
It can cause urethritis and/or proctitis, with a similar
purulent discharge to gonorrhoea, but tends to be 
far more invasive and can lead to severe 
complications (e.g., gangrene)

pages.label: Slide 21
pages.text:
Neisseria gonorrhoeae (gonorrhoea)
•
Neisseria gonorrhoeae is a Gram-negative species
of diplococcus-arranged, non-motile, non-spore-forming,
bacterium
•
Gonorrhoea is asymptomatic in around 
10% of men and >50% of women
•
It may cause painful/burning urination, 
unusual discharge (white/yellow/green) 
from the penis, vagina, rectum, anus, or throat
•
The incubation period is usually 2 – 8 days

pages.label: Slide 22
pages.text:
Chlamydia trachomatis (Chlamydia)
•
Chlamydia trachomatis is a species of 
Gram-negative, non-motile, 
coccus-shaped bacterium
•
Asymptomatic carriage is possible, 
with 50% and 80% of infected 
men and women reporting no 
symptoms, respectively
•
The bacterium can cause inflammation of the genital tract,
severe reproductive damage, infertility, conjunctivitis, 
reactive arthritis, urethritis, tonsilitis, swollen lymph glands, 
etc

pages.label: Slide 23
pages.text:
Shigella spp. (shigellosis)
•
Shigella is a genus of Gram-negative, non-motile, rod-shaped, 
facultative-anaerobic bacteria. Known to cause the faecal-oral, sexually
transmissible, bloody diarrhoeal disease: shigellosis (dysentery)
•
There are four species in the Shigella genus:
- Shigella sonnei
- Shigella flexneri
- Shigella boydii
- Shigella dysenteriae
•
Its inoculum dose is extraordinarily low (10 – 100 CFU)
•
Within each species, there may be more than one
serotype (e.g., Shigella flexneri 3a), defined by the
O-antigen repeat region of the cell wall lipopolysaccharide (LPS)
Shigella sonnei Gram-stain

pages.label: Slide 24
pages.text:
Shigella spp. symptoms
•
Species of the Shigella genus cause shigellosis, a severe
gastrointestinal illness characterised by bloody, potentially
mucus-filled, foul-smelling diarrhoea
•
Frequent passing of small volumes of diarrhoea is 
also common in shigellosis
•
A painful feeling of needing to empty the bowels, 
even when there is nothing left to excrete 
(tenesmus) is highly indicative of shigellosis
•
The incubation period can be as little as 24 hours
post-inoculation

pages.label: Slide 25
pages.text:
Shigella spp. diagnosis
•
As shigellosis presents as bloody diarrhoea, patients may
attend Accident & Emergency (A&E) in a hospital
rather than a sexual health clinic
•
Culturing of stool for Shigella spp. is the gold standard for 
shigellosis diagnosis
•
Molecular testing (PCR) is more rapid by identifying the ipaH gene, 
but caution is needed here as some E. coli may also carry this gene…
•
A major aid in diagnosing a patient with shigellosis is the context,
which is why it is important to ask the patient about their recent travel 
history and sexual activity history

Breast Cancer
•
Breast cancer is the most common cancer in the UK, despite the fact that it is rare in men. 
•
Breast cancer is by far the commonest cancer in women in the UK accounting for 31% of all 
cases in women and accounts for around 16% of female death (Cancer Research UK)
•
With the advent of the screening programme approximately 20% of  detected breast 
cancers are Ductal Carcinoma In Situ (DCIS). 
•
Evidence suggests that DCIS is the precursor to invasive breast cancer in most cases.  (JL Jones, 
2006, Br Ca Res)
•
Other studies have suggested that left untreated as many as 50% of DCIS cases will not 
progress in the life-time of the patient (L. Collins et al. 2005, Cancer; M Saunders et al, 2005, Cancer).

of cancer death in the

Ductal Carcinoma In Situ (DCIS)
• Non-invasive; confined within ducts, no basement 
membrane invasion
• Architectural patterns: comedo, cribriform, papillary, 
micropapillary, solid
• Comedo: central necrosis, high grade, calcifications
• Myoepithelial layer preserved; seen on H&E and 
confirmed by IHC
• Detected via mammographic microcalcifications

Lobular Carcinoma In Situ (LCIS)
• Non-invasive; confined to lobules/acini, no basement 
membrane invasion
• Usually incidental finding, often not associated with 
calcifications
• Architectural pattern: filling and distension of acini by small, 
uniform, dyshesive cells
• Cells: round nuclei, scant cytoplasm; loss of E-cadherin 
expression (IHC confirmation)
• Myoepithelial layer preserved
• Often multifocal and bilateral

Experiments:

The ability to determine cardiovascular variables such as blood pressure, heart rate, 
blood flow and cardiac output is essential in determining both an individual’s fitness 
and health.  Arterial blood pressure, can easily be measured without the need for 
invasive techniques and blood pressure can give us an indication of blood flow. 
Ambient temperature and ischaemia can both alter blood flow. Measurement of  BP 
can tell us about blood flow and factors affecting blood flow. 
Blood pressure is a variable that is determined by cardiac output and total peripheral 
resistance 
   mean arterial pressure = cardiac output X total peripheral resistance. 
                               (MAP=CO X TPR)
We can infer what may be happening to blood flow by observing whether

resistance to blood flow from all blood vessels, can be controlled by altering blood 
vessel diameter/radius (vasoconstriction or vasodilatation), and has a direct influence

resistance to flow and therefore will decrease blood pressure also.  In these 
experiments, arterial blood pressure will be measured by use of an electronic blood 
pressure monitor.
Heart rate can be measured by simple palpation at the wrist on the radial artery or 
using the electronic BP monitor. 
Aims of the Experiments
1. To determine the effect of temperature on arterial blood pressure and 
by inference, peripheral blood flow.
2. To determine the effect of recovery from ischaemia on arterial blood

Apparatus: hot water, ice, thermometer, blood pressure monitor, stopwatch
You will undertake these experiments working in groups of 5-6.
In this experiment you will determine the relationship between ambient (surrounding) 
temperature and arterial blood pressure.  The experiment is comprised of two parts, 
part 1 investigating effect of low (below body temp) temperature, part 2 investigating 
effect of high (above body temp) temperature.  A different person in each group 
should act as the subject for the first and second parts.
Part 1: Effect of cold water on BP (Cold pressor Test (CPT)):
Into the bucket/box provided, mix ice with tap water to achieve a temperature of       
5-60C. Make sure you stir well to distribute the temperature evenly.  Use the 
thermometer provided to make sure the temperature is 5-60C. Temperature must

Subject should sit down and relax.  Place the blood pressure monitor cuff around the  
upper arm, record systolic (SBP) & diastolic (DBP) BP to obtain an initial baseline

also give the pulse rate, record this as well on the proforma. 
The subject must then quietly rest for 2 minutes.

Introduction 
Single-gene disorders are conditions caused by mutations in a specific gene. Examples include cystic 
fibrosis, sickle cell anaemia, phenylketonuria, and Tay-Sachs disease. Molecular genetic testing for 
single-gene disorders is crucial in clinical practice as it provides an objective diagnosis, leading to 
proper patient management, facilitating genetic counselling, and potential prevention of disease 
transmission in future pregnancies. 
One of the widely used methods for the molecular genetic diagnosis of single-gene disorders is 
gene/mutation-targeted testing using Sanger sequencing. Despite the development of next-
generation sequencing (NGS) techniques, Sanger sequencing remains the gold standard test for 
many single-gene disorders due to its cost-effectiveness and quick turnaround time.  
Genetic disorders under investigation 
Each group of students will investigate one of the following disorders: 
1. Cystic fibrosis: an inherited disorder caused by biallelic mutations in the CFTR gene, which 
encodes a chloride channel protein. Mutations in the CFTR gene impair the folding and 
trafficking of the CFTR protein to the cell membrane, leading to reduced chloride transport 
and mucus accumulation in the lungs and other organs. 
2. Beta thalassaemia: an inherited blood disorder caused by mutations in the HBB gene, which 
encodes the beta-globin subunit of haemoglobin. These mutations reduce or abolish the 
production of beta-globin, leaving an excess of unpaired alpha-globin chains that damage 
the developing red blood cells and cause them to be destroyed prematurely. The result is a 
shortage of healthy red blood cells, leading to severe complications including anaemia, 
ineffective red blood cell production, enlargement of the spleen and liver, iron overload, 
susceptibility to infections, and damage to body organs. 
3. Phenylketonuria: an inherited disorder caused by biallelic mutations in the PAH gene, which 
encodes for the enzyme phenylalanine hydroxylase. The disorder inhibits the body’s ability 
to metabolize the essential amino acid phenylalanine, leading to an intolerance to dietary 
intake of phenylalanine. 
4. Tay-Sachs disease: an inherited disorder caused by biallelic mutations in the HEXA gene, 
which encodes the alpha subunit of the enzyme beta-hexosaminidase A. It results in the 
destruction of nerve cells in the brain and spinal cord.

Practical 1: DNA extraction 
Students will extract DNA from a cell sample of a patient with one of the above-mentioned 
diseases. 
Students should work individually. 
 
Part 1: Spin column genomic DNA preparation (Solution tubes are shared between 4 students): 
 
1. 
Label a 1.5ml ml tube of sample material (provided for you) with your initials & date. 
2. Centrifuge at 13000rpm, 4° C to pellet the cells. THIS STEP HAS BEEN DONE FOR YOU 
3. 
Pipette off the supernatant (Dispose of in waste bucket provided) 
4. 
Add 250 μl of the Resuspension Solution (with RNase A) to the tube. 
5. 
Resuspended the cells completely by vortexing until no cell clumps remain. 
6. 
Add 250 μl of the Lysis Solution to the tube. 
7. 
Mix thoroughly by inverting the tube 4-6 times. Do not vortex. 
8. 
Add 350 μl of the Neutralization Solution to the tube. 
9. 
Mix immediately and thoroughly by inverting the tube 4-6 times. 
10. 
Centrifuge for 5 minutes at 13,000 rpm. 
11. 
Label a GeneJET™ spin column, collection tube, and a 1.5 ml sample tube. 
12. 
Carefully, transfer the supernatant (containing the DNA) to the GeneJET™ spin 
column by pipetting. Avoid disturbing or transferring the white precipitate. This is best 
achieved by setting your P200 micropipette to 200 μl and gently removing 200 μl of the 
supernatant at a time. 
13. 
Centrifuge the GeneJET™ spin column for 1 minute at 13,000 rpm. 
14. 
Discard the flow-through and place the column back into the same collection tube. 
15. 
Add 500 μl of the Wash Solution (containing ethanol) to the GeneJET™ spin column. 
16. 
Centrifuge the GeneJET™ spin column for 1 minute at 13,000 rpm. 
17. 
Discard the flow-through and place the column back into the same collection tube. 
18. 
Add 500 μl of the Wash Solution (containing ethanol) to the GeneJET™ spin column. 
19. 
Centrifuge the GeneJET™ spin column for 1 minute at 13,000 rpm. 
20. 
Discard the flow-through and place the column back into the same collection tube. 
21. 
Centrifuge the GeneJET™ spin column for an additional 1 minute at 13,000 rpm.

• Potent metabolic stimuli to insulin secretion are glucose

Type 2 diabetes
Beta cells of the pancreas initially produce insulin but the body is unable to use it effectively 
because the cells of the body are resistant to the action of insulin. 
Diabetes is not simply a disease of high blood glucose, but a disease of impaired coordination 
between the major fuel stores and fuel-consuming tissues of the body.
Accounts for 90% of all diabetic individuals
- Complications include 
atherosclerosis, neurological changes, renal failure and blindness
In type 2 diabetes, insulin resistance disrupts whole-body fuel partitioning, so glucose is not 
effectively cleared by muscle while the liver continues to release glucose, causing a mismatch 
between substrate supply and utilization

pages.label: Slide 18

What is insulin resistance?
Insulin resistance is often defined based on measurements
of glucose metabolism
• The ability of insulin to reduce blood glucose is impaired (clearance) in blood
• The ability of insulin to reduce glucose production.
(production rate) in blood
Insulin also regulates the anabolism and storage of fat, protein synthesis, and 
non-metabolic process such as cell growth and differentiation. 
It is important to note that not all insulin-dependent processes and tissues are
equally resistant to insulin.

How was it technically 
achieved?
• Genetic and physical mapping
• A genetic map shows the location of genes 
on a genome, while a physical map shows 
the physical features of DNA molecules in 
chromosomes
• Genetic maps can help determine if a 
disease is linked to a gene and which 
chromosome it's on. Physical maps can help 
researchers determine the sequence of DNA 
base pairs

How was it technically 
achieved?
• Genetic mapping
• By using genetic markers, inherited physical or 
molecular characteristics that are different 
among individuals of a population.
• RFLP are an example of a genetic marker.
• Enzymes recognise short sequences of DNA & cut 
them at specific sites, cutting DNA into many 
different fragments.

Ethical, Legal, and Social Implications (ELSI): 
The HGP has prompted discussions about 
the ethical, legal, and social implications of 
genetic research, leading to the development 
of guidelines and policies to address issues

gene tests, reproductive issues and 
stigmatisation and discrimination.

Gregor Mendel developed the principles of segregation and independent assortment in the mid-1800s based on his detailed analysis of 
several traits in pea plants. Those principles, now called Mendel’s laws, in fact, explain the behavior of genes and alleles during meiosis 
and are now understood to underlie “Mendelian inheritance” of a wide range of traits and diseases across organisms. When asked to 
give examples of inheritance that do NOT follow Mendel’s laws, in other words, examples of non-Mendelian inheritance, students some­
times list incomplete dominance, codominance, multiple alleles, sex-linked traits, and multigene traits and cite as their sources the Khan 
Academy, Wikipedia, and other online sites. Against this background, the goals of this Perspective are to (1) explain to students, health­
care workers, and other stakeholders why the examples above, in fact, display Mendelian inheritance, as they obey Mendel’s laws of 
segregation and independent assortment, even though they do not produce classic Mendelian phenotypic ratios and (2) urge individuals 
with an intimate knowledge of genetic principles to monitor the accuracy of learning resources and work with us and those resources to 
correct information that is misleading.

The motivation for this Perspective
We were motivated to develop this Perspective by an anecdotal 
report that students were confused about the basis for cat­
egorizing inheritance as Mendelian vs non-Mendelian. That re­
port prompted us to survey students in undergraduate classes 
at several institutions on the categorization of various genetic 
phenomena (including complete dominance, incomplete 
dominance, codominance, multiple alleles, sex-linked traits, 
multigene traits, mitochondrial genes, and epigenetics) as dis­
playing Mendelian or non-Mendelian inheritance. Students 
were also asked to cite their source(s) of information. An over­
whelming majority (92%) of the 461 students surveyed correct­
ly classified completely dominant and recessive traits as 
following the rules of Mendelian inheritance. Disturbingly, a 
much smaller percentage of students across the 3 institutions 
(25–52% depending on the genetic example) correctly classified 
incomplete dominance, codominance, multiple alleles, sex- 
linked traits, and multigene traits as Mendelian, and some stu­
dents who misclassified those as non-Mendelian cited the 
Khan Academy, Wikipedia, and other online sites as their 
sources of information. Indeed, both the Khan Academy and 
Wikipedia list incomplete dominance, codominance, multiple 
alleles, and multigene traits as non-Mendelian. Why this con­
fusion? As developed below, we propose that the confusion 
stems from whether inheritance is categorized based on geno­
typic ratios or phenotypic ratios. We argue that inheritance 
should be classified as Mendelian or non-Mendelian based on 
genotypic, not phenotypic, ratios, since phenotypic ratios 
reflect the relationship between alleles rather than the mode 
of inheritance.
Introduction: what we learned from 
Mendel’s work
Mendel developed the principles of segregation, independent as­
sortment, and dominance based on his studies of 7 traits in 
peas, including flower color, pea color, and pea shape (Mendel 
1865-1866; Bateson 1909; Sturtevant 1965). The pea traits that 
Mendel focused on were determined by single genes, each of 
which had 2 alternativ alleles, 1 fully dominant and 1 fully reces­
sive. We now know that most traits in organisms are determined 
by multiple genes, that individual genes often have multiple al­
leles, and that some alleles display variations in dominance, in­
cluding 
incomplete 
dominance 
and 
codominance. 
The 
involvement of multiple genes, the possibility of multiple alleles, 
and unusual dominance relationships between different alleles 
do not influence how the 2 parental alleles of each gene are sorted 
into haploid gametes that fuse to form diploid offspring. Thus, the 
resulting offspring traits, whether in peas or other organisms, re­
sult from parental alleles that follow Mendel’s laws of segregation 
and independent assortment. Because of this, the inheritance pat­
terns of such traits are often discussed in Genetics textbooks as 
variations or extensions of Mendelian inheritance (e.g. Russell 
2010; Snustad and Simmons 2016; Pierce 2020; Brooker 2021; 
Goldberg et al. 2021). Because Mendel’s law of dominance does 
not impact how alleles are inherited but instead how they

Mendel’s laws of segregation and independent assortment to clas­

helpful discussion of dominance and recessiveness, see Zschocke 
et al. (2023).
The molecular basis of segregation and independent assort­
ment of alleles lies in the behavior of chromosomes during mei­
osis. Mendel did not know about chromosomes and meiosis, but 
the traits he studied and the principles he formulated beautifully 
and presciently predicted chromosome behavior in meiosis. In 
diploid organisms, like peas, the 2 versions of each chromosome, 
1 from each parent, segregate into the haploid gametes during 
meiosis. The union of 2 gametes at fertilization restores diploidy, 
with offspring inheriting 1 version of each chromosome from each 
parent. The pea traits or “phenotypes” that Mendel studied are 
dictated by genes that reside on chromosomes. The alleles of 
those genes segregate from each other into gametes during mei­
osis in the parents and are united at random in the offspring 
(Fig. 1a). This forms the basis for Mendel’s law of segregation. 
When different genes are on different chromosomes, as most of 
the pea genes studied by Mendel are, they behave independently 
of one another (Fig. 1b). This forms the basis for Mendel’s law of 
independent assortment. The power of our now-deep under­
standing of meiosis is the ability to predict offspring genotypes 
and phenotypes and their ratios that parents will produce. 
Indeed, in Mendel’s experiments, he observed that crossing 
true-breeding plants with purple flowers (P/P) and true-breeding 
plants with white flowers (p/p) generated all plants with purple 
flowers (P/p); crossing those P/p plants with one another gener­
ated 1/4 P/P purple-flower plants, 2/4 P/p purple-flower plants, 
and 1/4 p/p white-flower plants (Fig. 2a).
Mendel’s published studies (Mendel 1865-1866) focused on 2 
versions of each of the pea plant traits he studied. For example, 
for flower color, the dominant P allele led to purple flowers, and 
the recessive p allele led to white flowers. We now understand 
the molecular biology for some of those traits and the basis for 
some of them, such as flower color, to display variations beyond 
those studied by Mendel (Ellis et al. 2011). Notably, Mendel’s focus 
on single-gene, 2-allele traits derived from clear dominant and re­
cessive relationships enabled him to develop the laws of segrega­
tion and independent assortment. It is a tribute to Mendel that he 
accurately deduced the transmission of genes and alleles from 
parents to offspring based on analyzing the phenotypes of parents 
and offspring. That has led to some confusion about whether 
genotypic ratios or phenotypic ratios should dictate whether in­
heritance is described as Mendelian or non-Mendelian. In this 
Perspective, we discuss the reasoning behind our opinion that 
Mendelian inheritance should always be distinguished based on 
genotypic ratios that derive from segregation and independent as­
sortment during meiosis.
In addition to Mendel’s laws of segregation and independent 
assortment, Mendel’s work led to the recognition of 2 additional 
features of inheritance: that alleles are passed unaltered through 
multiple generations (even through generations in which a reces­
sive allele does not display its phenotype due to the presence of a 
dominant allele), and that the phenotypes of individuals are dic­
tated by their genotypes. We discuss how some examples of 
non-Mendelian inheritance violate these inheritance features.
Extensions of Mendel’s laws and variations 
in phenotypic ratios
In Mendel’s studies of pea traits, from crosses between heterozy­
gous parents (e.g. P/p crossed with P/p), the offspring showed a 
1:2:1 genotypic ratio (1 P/P : 2 P/p : 1 p/p) and a 3:1 phenotypic ratio 
(3 purple:1 white; Fig. 2a). The relationships between alleles that 
underlie variations in dominance, the existence of more than 2 al­
leles of a gene, sex-linked traits, and multigene traits result in

the 2 alleles of each gene in an individual still follow the law of 
segregation during meiosis and still produce Mendelian genotypic 
ratios in offspring, thus displaying Mendelian inheritance. This 
can be seen in Punnett squares (Fig. 1), branch diagrams, and ped­
igrees (Fig. 3a) showing the passage of alleles from parents to off­
spring. Below are examples of each, taken from and developed 
more fully in the textbook “Genetics: From Genes to Genomes” 
7th edition by Goldberg et al. (2021).
Incomplete dominance
In cases of incomplete dominance, the phenotype of a heterozy­
gote with 2 different alleles of a gene is intermediate between 
the phenotypes of the homozygotes. An example is flower color 
in snap dragons (Fig. 2b). Homozygotes for an allele that causes 
the production of red pigment have red flowers. Homozygotes 
for an allele that does not produce pigment have white flowers. 
Heterozygotes with a red-producing allele and a white allele are 
pink, which is intermediate in color between red and white. This 
is because in heterozygotes, only 1 allele produces pigment, which 
is enough to make flowers pink but not enough to make them red. 
(In the case of pea flower color where the P allele shows complete 
dominance, in heterozygous P/p plants, 1 P allele is sufficient to 
make the flowers purple.) When plants with pink flowers are 
crossed together, the next generation of plants display all 3 flower 
colors in the ratio of 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white. Thus, from crossing 
heterozygous snapdragons, both the genotypic and the phenotyp­
ic ratios are 1:2:1. The alleles that control snapdragon flower color 
segregate properly to gametes during meiosis and thus follow 
Mendel’s law of segregation. The phenotypic ratio is different 
from what Mendel saw for pea flower color, because the down­
stream relationship between the 2 alleles of the flower-color 
gene in heterozygotes and the pigment produced differ between 
peas and snap dragons.
Codominance
In cases of codominance, the phenotypes caused by 2 different al­
leles of the same gene are both expressed. An example is the hu­
man AB blood type (Fig. 2c). The human blood type is 
determined by the I gene. The A allele of the gene (called IA) causes 
red blood cells to have the A sugar on their cell surface. The B al­
lele (IB) causes red blood cells to have the B sugar on their surface. 
The IA and IB alleles are codominant: IA/IB individuals have both 
the A and the B sugars on their red blood cells and therefore 
have an AB blood type. Thus, from a cross of IA/IB heterozygotes, 
both the genotypic ratio and the phenotypic ratio observed in off­
spring are 1:2:1. Once again, although the phenotypic ratio is not 
the 3:1 of Mendel’s pea flowers, the 2 alleles of the I gene in an in­
dividual segregate according to Mendel’s law. It is the relationship 
between the gene products from the alleles that produces varia­
tions in phenotypes, particularly in heterozygotes.
Multiple alleles
Many genes have more than 2 alleles in a population of indivi­
duals. An example is the agouti gene in mice, which has at least 
19 alleles (Bultman et al. 1992). Importantly, individual mice 
have only 2 alleles, and those 2 alleles (whatever those 2 alleles 
may be) are transmitted in a Mendelian fashion. The alleles dis­
play a dominance series; for example, the A allele is dominant 
to the at allele and the a allele, and the at allele is dominant to 
the a allele. The agouti locus regulates the distribution of yellow 
and black pigment in mouse fur on the back and belly. The various 
combinations of alleles cause mice to have coat colors that range 
from black to gray to yellow, sometimes with different coloration 
on the back and belly. The 2 alleles from each parent are

The AY allele of the mouse agouti gene illustrates an additional 
lesson about genes and alleles. The AY allele in heterozygotes, in 
combination with any of the other agouti alleles (e.g. AY/A), causes 
mice to have yellow fur, while the AY allele in homozygotes 
(AY/AY) causes mice to die during gestation (Fig. 2d). Thus, the 
AY allele has a dominant effect on coat color and a recessive effect 
on viability. This underscores that the dominant–recessive rela­
tionship of 2 alleles of a gene depends on the phenotype being 
analyzed. Importantly, from a cross of AY/A parents, the genotyp­
ic ratio in embryos is 1:2:1 due to Mendelian segregation, but the 
lethality of AY/AY embryos during in utero development skews 
the coat-color phenotypic ratio observed in viable offspring to 2:1.
An appreciation of the diversity of allele types and interactions 
is emerging from the isolation of many alleles of heavily studied 
genes (e.g. the mouse agouti gene; Bultman et al. 1992) and the 
now-common use of high-throughput genome sequencing in de­
velopmental and medical genetics (Zschocke et al. 2023). These 
and a number of earlier studies make clear that allele assign­
ments may be more complicated than simply dominant or reces­
sive, and that phenotypes are dictated by often-complex 
contributions of multiple allele pairs. These unusual relationships 
highlight the need for an unambiguous and clear understanding 
of the underlying Mendelian inheritance principles by scientists 
and especially health professionals.
Sex-linked traits
Sex-linked traits in organisms commonly discussed in genetics 
courses, namely humans and fruit flies, deal with genes on the 
X chromosome and, less frequently, genes on the Y chromosome. 
Two examples are red-green color blindness and some forms of 
hemophilia in humans. The genes for these 2 traits reside on 
the X chromosome. The phenotypes caused by mutant alleles 
of the genes are more commonly observed in males with a 
single X chromosome than in females with 2 X chromosomes. 
Considering hemophilia (Fig. 3a), if H is the dominant normal allele 
and h is a recessive mutant allele that causes hemophilia, females 
that are XH/XH or XH/Xh will not have hemophilia, while females 
that are Xh/Xh and males that are Xh/Y will have hemophilia. This 
results in interesting phenotypic ratios of affected offspring in ped­
igrees. For example, an unaffected father (XH/Y) and an unaffected 
heterozygous mother (XH/Xh) can have some affected sons (Xh/Y) 
and some unaffected sons (XH/Y), but none of their daughters 
(XH/Xh and XH/XH) will be affected. Since the X and Y chromosomes 
and their resident genes segregate from each other during meiosis, 
X- and Y-linked traits display Mendelian inheritance.

served by Mendel for the P gene alone. The 9:7 phenotypic ratio 
from crossing P/p; C/c plants arises because offspring homozy­
gous for a mutant allele of either gene (e.g. p/p or c/c) produce 
white flowers (Fig. 3b). This example demonstrates that when 2 
unlinked genes influence a single trait, Mendel’s laws of segrega­
tion and independent assortment commonly result in phenotypic 
ratios that diverge from the classic 9:3:3:1.
Another example of genes acting in a pathway is coat color in 
Labrador retrievers, which relies on the E gene for the production 
of the black pigment eumelanin and the B gene for dense depos­
ition of eumelanin in dog hairs (Fig. 3c). Labradors that produce 
eumelanin and deposit it densely are black. Labradors that pro­
duce eumelanin but cannot deposit it densely are brown or choc­
olate in color. Labradors that cannot produce eumelanin are 
yellow. The E and B genes are unlinked, and the alleles of both 
genes are transmitted in Mendelian fashion; when considered as 
single genes, offspring from heterozygous parents display a 1:2:1 
genotypic ratio. It is the different combinations of alleles of the 
2 genes that determine the 3 different coat-color phenotypes. 
This example illustrates a phenomenon termed “epistasis,” in 
which mutations in 1 gene mask the effects of a second gene 
(Miko 2008). In Labradors, the inability to produce eumelanin 
masks our seeing whether eumelanin can be deposited; this shifts 
the phenotypic ratio from 9:3:3:1 to 9:3:4 (Fig. 3c). Epistasis is 
sometimes mistakenly considered to be an example of non- 
Mendelian inheritance, but the individual alleles involved follow 
the laws of segregation and independent assortment perfectly 
and thus display Mendelian inheritance.
Many human traits such as height and skin color and conditions 
such as schizophrenia and autism are determined by numerous 
genes and are often classified as quantitative or continuous traits. 
Particularly when the number and identity of the genes involved 
are not known, inheritance patterns of these polygenic traits 
and conditions are difficult to predict. Furthermore, the pheno­
types associated with many of these traits and conditions may 
be influenced by external factors including the environment. 
Nevertheless, the inheritance of alleles of these genes follow 
Mendel’s laws of segregation and independent assortment.
Linkage
The above examples illustrate the behavior of alleles of genes that 
reside on different chromosomes. Genes that are on the same 
chromosome (i.e. linked) violate Mendel’s law of independent as­
sortment due to physical linkage. Nevertheless, they display pat­
terns of inheritance that can be predicted once the genes have 
been genetically mapped with relation to one another and the fre­
quency of recombination between them has been quantified. 
Thus, even linked genes display Mendelian inheritance.
Some examples of non-Mendelian 
inheritance
Genes that reside in the genomes of mitochondria and chloro­
plasts display non-Mendelian inheritance. The segregation of 
such non-nuclear organelles and the alleles in their genomes is 
thought to be largely random during the meiotic divisions. In 
many organisms and in most animals, these organelles and their 
resident genes are inherited by offspring mainly from the female 
parent (e.g. Giles et al. 1980; Sato and Sato 2013). Because organelle 
transmission does not follow Mendel’s laws, the genes in orga­
nelles do not display Mendelian inheritance.
Epigenetic inheritance provides another example of non- 
Mendelian inheritance. Epigenetics refers to the regulation of 
gene expression and development by factors beyond the DNA 
sequence. The most heavily studied epigenetic regulators are DNA 
methylation, histone modifications, and small RNAs (reviewed in 
Allis et al. 2015). These regulators participate in such phenomena 
as genomic imprinting, paramutation, creation of epialleles, and 
RNA interference (Heard and Martienssen 2014; Fitz-James and 
Cavalli 2022; Yoosefzadeh Najafabadi et al. 2023 ). Epigenetic mark­
ing of genes by DNA methylation and histone modifications is 
subject to removal and addition in each generation in response to 
developmental cues and environmental influences, unlike the 
underlying DNA sequence. Because epigenetic marking is not 
passed unaltered through multiple generations, inheritance of the 
marks is considered non-Mendelian.
Maternal-effect genetics describes situations in which the phe­
notypes of individuals are dictated not by their genotypes but by 
the genotype of their mother. This is exemplified by the inherit­
ance of snail coiling patterns (Sturtevant 1923) and by maternal 
control of early embryonic development in fruit flies (e.g. 
Nüsslein-Volhard et al. 1987). The logic behind this is that the ma­
ternal genotype dictates which gene products are packaged into 
oocytes, and those gene products dictate events in early embryos 
until embryos start generating gene products from their own gen­
ome (when zygotic transcription turns on). Because offspring de­
velopment depends on the maternal genotype instead of the 
offspring’s genotype, maternal-effect inheritance is considered 
non-Mendelian.
Interestingly, there are biological phenomena in which Mendelian 
inheritance of nuclear genes is distorted such that some alleles are 
preferentially transmitted to offspring. These phenomena, called 
“meiotic drive,” can act at different stages of gamete production 
and function to deliberately skew allele inheritance (Srinivasa 
and Zanders 2020). For example, in some maize plants, there 
are loci of repetitive DNA that cause heterochromatic “knobs,” 
so named because of their cytological appearance (McClintock 
1930). Chromosomes with knobs can be homozygous, heterozy­
gous, or absent in plants. When knob-bearing chromosomes are 
heterozygous in plants that also have a chromosome called “abnor­
mal chromosome 10” (Ab10), knob chromosomes are preferentially 
segregated to the ovule, the sole gamete produced by female mei­
osis, with the other products of meiosis being discarded as polar 
bodies (Dawe 2022). Thus, more than 70% rather than the expected 
50% of ovules carry knob chromosomes and their linked alleles, a 
clear distortion of Mendel’s law of segregation (Rhoades 1942).
Some other versions of meiotic drive act after meiotic chromo­
some segregation; these include the Segregation Distorter locus in 
fruit flies (Larracuente and Presgraves 2012) and the t-haplotype 
in mice (Herrmann et al. 1999). In both of these examples, sperm 
that do not carry the locus associated with drive fail to develop 
properly, preventing their ability to participate in fertilization.

Thus, sperm with the drive locus fertilize more eggs and produce 
more offspring than sperm without the drive locus. Meiotic drive 
phenomena provide fascinating molecular and evolutionary in­
sights into how specific loci use “selfish” mechanisms to produce 
biased allele inheritance, in clear violation of Mendel’s laws.
The importance of understanding 
Mendelian inheritance
The main message of this Perspective is that categorizing patterns 
of inheritance as Mendelian or non-Mendelian should be based on 
genotypic ratios, not phenotypic ratios, in offspring. Genotypic ra­
tios reflect the segregation and independent assortment of alleles 
during meiosis in parents, which are the underpinnings of 
Mendel’s laws, while phenotypic ratios reflect the modes of action 
of the gene products and the relationships between alleles in off­
spring. Categorizing patterns of inheritance as Mendelian or 
non-Mendelian is not strictly an issue of semantics, but instead 
is based on an understanding of the various genetic situations 
that follow Mendel’s laws but may produce unusual phenotypes 
in offspring. Textbooks describe these situations as extensions 
or variations of Mendelian inheritance (e.g. Russell 2010; 
Snustad and Simmons 2016; Pierce 2020; Brooker 2021; Goldberg 
et al. 2021). This Perspective makes clear why they are not viola­
tions of Mendelian inheritance.
Social media and online sites such as the Khan Academy and 
Wikipedia are valued and appreciated for providing accessible in­
formation quickly and efficiently and being receptive to input 
from the community. However, given their reliance on volunteers 
and crowdsourcing, they may provide incorrect or biased informa­
tion. Therefore, community input should include experts moni­
toring 
the 
accuracy 
of 
the 
information 
and 
clarifying 
information that is misleading. Health care is 1 arena in which 
having access to accurate and easy-to-understand information 
is crucial. Primary-care providers must understand and be able 
to explain to patients and their families basic genetic concepts 
that underlie conditions and diseases, to help them make 
informed decisions (Houwink et al. 2011). Other stakeholders 
who need accurate online genetic information include anthropol­
ogists, ecologists, forensic pathologists, conservation biologists, 
commercial plant and animal breeders, and individuals 
involved in captive breeding programs for endangered species. 
Furthermore, to avoid confusion, students need accurate online 
information on basic Mendelian concepts that reinforces textbook 
and classroom information. Understanding the fundamental dif­
ference between genotypic and phenotypic ratios is essential to 
fully appreciate the extent to which specific traits are genetically 
determined and for informed discussions of more complex, socio­
politically constructed phenomena, such as race and gender, that 
move away from genetic determinism (Donovan, Weindling, et al. 
2024; Donovan, Syed, et al. 2024; Duncan et al. 2024).
The authors of this Perspective plan to work with the Khan 
Academy, Wikipedia, and other online sites to clarify Mendelian 
vs non-Mendelian inheritance. We urge informed community 
members to join this effort and invite them to contact us with 
strategy and coordination ideas.

Good microbiological practice 
& Containment #2
• When handling micro-organism aseptic 
techniques should be used at all times.
• Why?
– To prevent contamination of the laboratory 
or personnel by the organisms being 
handled
– To prevent contamination of the organisms 
from the environment or handler

pages.label: Slide 10
pages.text:
• Aseptic techniques include: 
– No mouth pipetting.
– No eating, drinking, smoking or applying makeup 
or mobiles.
– General tidiness and cleanliness: 
• Cleaning up spillage with suitable agent. 
– Placing used pipette in disinfectant tip down.
– Clearly label all specimens.
– Loops sterilised immediately after use in Bunsen 
flame and ensuring the loop is not overload to 
prevent spitting.
– Wash hand before leaving the laboratory.
– No open toes or soft fabric shoes.
– Designated Micro lab coat and safety glass

pages.label: Slide 11
pages.text:
• Aseptic techniques include: 
– Avoid creation of aerosols:
o Don’t blow material from pipettes.
o Don’t shake cultures too vigorously.
o Don’t expose culture to air for too long.
o Care should be taken with post-mortem dissection.
o Care when grinding/homogenisation tissue.
o Care when centrifugation – tube should be well sealed.

Adipose tissue
Cushions internal organs and insulates the body. Swell as they store fat and shrink when the fat is used for

Inheritance
• Pea plant experiments led to the formation of Mendel’s 
Laws widely known as the Laws of Inheritance, which are:
• Law of Segregation

pages.label: Slide 5
pages.text:
Law of Segregation
• Every organism has two 
alleles for each trait, and 
these alleles separate 
during meiosis, resulting 
in each gamete carrying 
only one of the alleles. 
Consequently, an 
offspring inherits a pair 
of alleles for a trait by 
receiving one allele from 
each parent.

pages.label: Slide 6
pages.text:
Law of independent 
assortment
• Unlinked or distantly linked 
segregating gene pairs 
operate independently. 
Alleles for different traits are 
transmitted independently of 
each other. The selection of 
an allele for one trait does 
not influence the selection of 
an allele for another trait.

pages.label: Slide 8
pages.text:
Law of Dominance
• When the two alleles of an 
inherited pair are 
different, this is known as 
a heterozygous condition. 
One allele, which defines 
the organism's 
appearance, is referred to 
as the dominant allele, 
while the other allele, 
which does not have a 
visible impact on the 
organism's appearance, is 
termed the recessive 
allele.

Multiple long-term conditions (MLTC): Living with two or more chronic illnesses. 
For example, a person could have diabetes, heart disease and depression at the 
same time. 
Multimorbidity can have a significant impact on people's health and wellbeing. It 
also poses a complex challenge to healthcare systems which are traditionally 
focused on individual diseases.
Multiple long-term conditions are much more common in older people, affecting 
more than half of those over 65, however, they can also be found in young 
people.
Khunti K, Sathanapally H, Mountain P. (2023) Multiple long term conditions, multimorbidity, and co-morbidities: we should 
reconsider the terminology we use. BMJ. Oct 13;383:2327

Who is at risk? 
People of all age groups, regions and countries are affected by NCDs. These 
conditions are often associated with older age groups, but data shows that 17 
million NCD deaths occur before the age of 70 years. 
https://www.who.int/data/gho/data/themes/noncommunicable-diseases

What is the cause of these 
diseases?
A combination of physiological, environmental, 
behavioural and genetic factors.
NCDs are driven by forces that include rapid,

Ageing population

individuals carry

Modifiable are the major risk factors for the most common NCDs
Smoking, physical inactivity, unhealthy diet and the harmful use of 
alcohol, all increase the risk of NCDs.
Tobacco accounts for over 8 million deaths every year (including 
from the effects of exposure to second-hand smoke) (1).
1.8 million annual deaths have been attributed to excess

L E A R N I N G  O B J E C T I V E S
By the end of this lecture, you should be able to:
• List the different types of normal variation that occur between human 
genomes
• Provide examples of sequence, length, and structural polymorphisms
• Explain why normal genetic variation is a useful research tool in human 
genetics
• Describe the tracking of genetic fragments through linkage disequilibrium, 
haplotypes, and haplogroups

pages.text: W H E R E  A R E  W E ? ?

pages.label: Slide 4
pages.text:
H O W  D O  H U M A N  G E N O M E S  D I F F E R ?
Similar but different
We know that any two randomly 
selected humans share ~99% of 
their DNA sequence and structure
Put differently, the sequence and 
structure of your own genome is 
about 99% similar to the 
reference human genome
What sorts of differences make 
up the remaining percentage?

pages.label: Slide 5
pages.text:
H O W  D O  H U M A N  G E N O M E S  D I F F E R ?
Pathogenic vs polymorphic
Variation between genomes ranges 
from single nucleotide differences 
to gains and losses of whole 
chromosomes
Normal, polymorphic variation is 
limited to:
Sequence polymorphisms
Length polymorphisms
Structural polymorphisms
(Epigenetic differences)

pages.label: Slide 6
pages.text:
S E Q U E N C E  P O L Y M O R P H I S M S
Snip snip….
The most common type of 
sequence polymorphism is a single 
nucleotide polymorphism (SNP)
SNPs generally arise as single 
nucleotide replication errors 
passed down for several 
generations
A SNP occurs once in every 100-
300 bases
Each of us has about 11 million 
SNPs in our genome

pages.label: Slide 7
pages.text:
S E Q U E N C E  P O L Y M O R P H I S M S
Cataloguing SNPs
More than 100+ million SNPs 
are known
Most SNPs occur in non-coding 
sequence
SNPs are stable differences 
between genomes, making them 
useful tools for examining 
different genomes

pages.label: Slide 8
pages.text:
L E N G T H  P O L Y M O R P H I S M S
How long is a piece of DNA?
Length polymorphisms involve changes in 
frequency of a repeat unit
Over 50% of the genome is repetitive 
sequence
Repeated DNA sequences either occur in 
tandem (next door to each other) or are 
interspersed
Length polymorphisms refer mainly to 
tandem repeats

pages.label: Slide 9
pages.text:
L E N G T H  P O L Y M O R P H I S M S
Why why so so repetitive?
Replication of DNA is error prone
DNA polymerases can lose track of 
how many repeats have been 
replicated and how many await 
replication
When polymerase slips backward, 
new repeats are added (insertion). 
When polymerase slips forwards, 
some repeats are left out (deletion)

pages.label: Slide 10
pages.text:
L E N G T H  P O L Y M O R P H I S M S
An unfair exchange
Aligning and recombining 
DNA is also error prone
Misaligned repeats can 
either cause unequal 
sister chromatid 
exchange (between 
strands of replicated 
DNA) or unequal 
crossover (between 
replicated chromosomes

pages.label: Slide 11
pages.text:
L E N G T H  P O L Y M O R P H I S M S
Size matters
The size of the repeated 
DNA sequence unit can 
range from 1 nucleotide, to 
over 1 million nucleotides!
Size ranges are given 
different names to help 
distinguish them

pages.label: Slide 12
pages.text:
L E N G T H  P O L Y M O R P H I S M S
Homopolymer
A homopolymer, or a 
homopolymer tract, is a 1 
nucleotide repeat unit
AAAA
GGGGGGG
TTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTT
Number of repeats: 4
Repeat unit size: 1 base
Number of repeats: 7
Number of repeats: 20

pages.label: Slide 13
pages.text:
L E N G T H  P O L Y M O R P H I S M S
Microsatellites
A microsatellite is a repeat 
unit consisting of 2-10 
bases
ATATATAT
GCGGCGGCGGCGGCG
Repeat unit size: 2 bases
Repeat unit size: 3 bases
Number of repeats: 4
Number of repeats: 5

pages.label: Slide 14
pages.text:
L E N G T H  P O L Y M O R P H I S M S
Other satellites
Minisatellites have a repeat 
unit of 11-100 bases
Satellites have a repeat unit 
of  ~100-400 bases
The entire segment of DNA 
consisting of a repeat motif 
is referred to as an array

pages.label: Slide 15
pages.text:
L E N G T H  P O L Y M O R P H I S M S
More terminology
Some arrays are fixed in size and don’t vary 
from one person to the next
However, most homopolymers, 
microsatellite, minisatellite, and  satellite 
arrays vary in size and are collectively 
referred to as variable number tandem 
repeats (VNTRs) or short tandem repeats 
(STRs)
VNTRs/STRs are the typical example of 
length polymorphisms

pages.label: Slide 16
pages.text:
S T R U C T U R A L  P O L Y M O R P H I S M S
An a-maize-ing discovery
Repeat units can also be interspersed 
throughout the genome, rather than occurring 
in tandem
Most of these interspersed repeats are 
transposons
A transposon is a DNA segment that can 
change its position in the genome (also known 
as a jumping gene or a mobile genetic element)

pages.label: Slide 17
pages.text: S T R U C T U R A L  P O L Y M O R P H I S M S

pages.label: Slide 18
pages.text:
S T R U C T U R A L  P O L Y M O R P H I S M S
Signs and lines
There are two main families of transposons
Short interspersed nuclear elements (SINEs)
Long interspersed nuclear elements (LINEs)

pages.label: Slide 19
pages.text:
S T R U C T U R A L  P O L Y M O R P H I S M S
Littered lines
Transposable elements are scattered throughout your entire 
genome, even between exons!
Most transposons in the human genome no longer “jump”

pages.label: Slide 20
pages.text:
S T R U C T U R A L  P O L Y M O R P H I S M S
Do you copy?
Any repeat unit (whether tandem or 
interspersed) larger than 50 bases 
that shows variation between 
individuals is also known as a copy 
number variant (CNV)
Changes in the copy number of 
CNVs occur as the result of 
structural changes (insertion, 
deletion, translocation, duplication, 
inversion), and can thus be referred 
to as structural polymorphisms

pages.label: Slide 21
pages.text: S T R U C T U R A L  P O L Y M O R P H I S M S

pages.label: Slide 22
pages.text:
P O L Y M O R P H I S M S
The special case of indels
Insertions and deletions (indels) of non-repeat motif DNA sequence sit at the 
intersection between sequence, length, and structural polymorphisms.
Indels can range in size from 1 base to entire chromosome segments
These can affect the sequence, length, and structure of the DNA

pages.label: Slide 23
pages.text: N O R M A L  V A R I A T I O N

pages.label: Slide 24
pages.text:
N O R M A L  V A R I A T I O N
Unique, just like 
everyone else
Understanding the ways in 
which genomes differ 
normally can be used to 
our advantage
Human identification
Paternity and kinship 
testing
Human history and 
evolution
Disease susceptibility

pages.label: Slide 25
pages.text:
P O P U L A T I O N  G E N E T I C S
Keeping track of what’s normal
Population genetics is the study of genetic variation within and between 
populations, and how this variation is maintained or changed over time.

pages.label: Slide 26
pages.text:
P O P U L A T I O N  G E N E T I C S
What is a population?
A biological population is any group of members of the same species, living in the same 
geographical region, that interbreed or can potentially interbreed
To study genetic variation within a population, we need to count the amount of normal 
variation and determine how much this changes from one generation to the next
To do this, we first need to recall how genetic material is inherited

pages.label: Slide 27
pages.text:
T H E  P R O C E S S  O F  I N H E R I T A N C E
Taking chunks from the gene pool
DNA is inherited in “chunks” 
Homologous chromosomes undergo recombination, so that the offspring receives 
a mixture of genetic material

pages.label: Slide 28
pages.text:
P O P U L A T I O N  G E N E T I C S
A family affair
The global population is one large 
family
A chunk of DNA that is inherited as a 
unit (more commonly than statistics 
would predict) is known as a linkage 
disequilibrium block
Linkage – the DNA sequence is linked 
together to form a unit
Disequilibrium – the chunk of DNA is 
passed on as a whole unit more often 
than statistics would predict

pages.label: Slide 29
pages.text:
P O P U L A T I O N  G E N E T I C S
Chunk tracking
Because DNA is inherited in chunks that can stay intact for many generations, we can often identify 
chunks by just examining the normal variants on each chunk, instead of having to read the whole 
sequence
Since SNPs are so common in the human genome (1 every 100-300 bases), we can take note of which 
groups of SNPs seem to be inherited together more often than you would expect
This group of SNPs is called a haplotype -  a set of closely linked markers that are inherited together

pages.label: Slide 30
pages.text: P O P U L A T I O N  G E N E T I C S

pages.label: Slide 31
pages.text:
P O P U L A T I O N  G E N E T I C S
Short hand
Haplotypes are a “shortcut” for 
referring to a much larger chunk of 
DNA
Similar haplotypes can be grouped 
together into “haplogroups”
When studying populations, we 
determine the frequency of normal 
variants, haplotypes, and/or 
haplogroups. This can be done in 
autosomes, sex chromosomes, or 
the mitochondrial genome

pages.label: Slide 32
pages.text:
P O P U L A T I O N  G E N E T I C S
Uniparental inheritance
Tracking haplotypes and haplogroups in the mitochondrial genome and the non-
recombining portion of the Y chromosome is how ancestry testing is done for 
your maternal and paternal heritage respectively.

pages.label: Slide 33
pages.text: P O P U L A T I O N  G E N E T I C S

pages.label: Slide 34
pages.text: P O P U L A T I O N  G E N E T I C S

pages.label: Slide 35
pages.text:
P O P U L A T I O N  G E N E T I C S
Adam and Eve
Theoretically, we could track the mitochondrial lineage of all extant humans back 
to one woman (mitochondrial Eve) and the non-recombining portion of the Y 
chromosome to one man (Y-chromosome Adam)

pages.label: Slide 36
pages.text:
P O P U L A T I O N  G E N E T I C S
A more complicated story
Common misconceptions about mt-Eve 
and Y-MRCA reveal how challenging it is 
to conceptualise and track human 
history:
Not the only man/woman alive at the 
time
Not one fixed individual
Not alive at the same time as each other
Not the most recent common ancestor 
shared by all humans

pages.label: Slide 37
pages.text:
P O P U L A T I O N  G E N E T I C S
One small piece of a much larger puzzle
Tracking only patrilineal and matrilineal heritage excludes the majority of the 
human genome
Population genetics must also have methods for tracking autosomal variation…but 
how?

pages.label: Slide 38
pages.text:
S U M M A R Y
• Normal variation in the human genome can be loosely 
categorised into sequence, length, and structural 
polymorphisms
• Identifying and cataloguing normal variation between 
humans provides a useful tool for several different functions
• Population genetics is the discipline concerned with studying 
normal genetic variation and how it is maintained or 
changed over time
• It is easiest to track variation in non-recombining portions of 
the genome, but this has limited scope

🔬Scientific Method: Hypothesis Formation
In the scientific method, after observing a phenomenon, the researcher formulates a 
hypothesis - a testable prediction about the relationship between variables.
It’s focused, aiming to validate or refute a specific claim through experimentation.
Example: ‘The novel anti-inflammatory drug will reduce joint inflammation in rheumatoid 
arthritis.’
 
🎨Design Thinking: Define Stage
Design thinking is about framing a problem based on insights gathered during the empathise 
phase.
It’s open-ended and human-centered, aiming to understand the broader context and needs 
of users and stakeholders.
Instead of a hypothesis, it produces a problem statement that guides ideation.
Example: ‘Patients with rheumatoid arthritis struggle to access treatments that are both 
effective and affordable.’

pages.label: Slide 4
pages.text:
What is the healthcare/scientific definition 
of ‘sterile’?
• The standard definition used in healthcare and 
microbiology is: “free from any viable 
microorganisms or endospores”
• For medical devices (catheters, syringes, 
etc.), manufacturers must meet a Sterility 
Assurance Level (SAL) of 10-6
• This means there is no more than a 
1 in 1,000,000 probability of a viable
organism being on a piece of sterilised equipment

pages.label: Slide 5
pages.text:
What is the food industry definition of ‘sterile’?
• In food microbiology, the term ‘commercial 
sterility’ is commonly used
• In this case, ‘sterile’ does not mean
‘free from all viable microorganisms
or endospores’ 
• It means that: ‘microorganisms capable
of growing under the normal storage 
conditions of the product have been 
eliminated’

pages.label: Slide 7
pages.text:
Moist heat steam sterilisation (autoclaving)
• Denatures and coagulates proteins / nucleic acids
• High temperature (121°C)
• Short length of time  (15 minutes)
• High pressure (15 psi)
• Eliminates all viruses,
bacteria, fungi, protists,
helminths, & endospores

pages.label: Slide 8
pages.text:
Checking heat sterilisation conditions have
been reached
• Physical methods of checking:
- Thermocouples data loggers (show temperature)
- Pressure gauges and transducers (show pressure)
- Autoclave printouts (time, temp., pressure history)
• Chemical methods of checking:
- Autoclave tape shows conditions were reached
- Browne’s tubes show conditions were reached
(Red  Green colour change)
• Biological methods of checking:
- Use Geobacillus stearothermophilus spores
as a control to see if autoclaving is working correctly

pages.label: Slide 9
pages.text:
Dry heat sterilisation
• Works via causing oxidative 
damage and protein denaturation
• 160-180°C for 2 to 3 hours(!)
• Used extensively on glassware, 
metal instruments, powders, oils
• Think critically – why not use
steam on those products instead?

pages.label: Slide 10
pages.text:
Incineration sterilisation
• Extremely high temperature 
(>800°C)
• Complete combustion of
microorganisms and materials
• Used to destroy disposable loops, 
L-shaped spreaders, plastics, and 
any clinical waste

pages.label: Slide 11
pages.text:
Direct flaming sterilisation
• Use of a Bunsen burner flame
with a nichrome microbiological
loop (which reaches 700°C-1000°C)
• Rapid oxidation and burning of the
material on the loop
• Used extensively in academic,
clinical, and commercial settings

pages.label: Slide 12
pages.text:
Filtration (membrane sterilisation)
• Typically using a 0.22μm filter
(20 nm used to filter out viruses!)
• Physically removes 
microorganisms
from a sample
• Primarily used in antibiotic 
solutions, vaccines, serum, 
and heat-sensitive media

pages.label: Slide 13
pages.text:
High-Efficiency Particulate Air Filter (HEPA)
sterilisation 
• ≥99.97% removal of 0.3μm particles
• Physically removes airborne 
microorganisms…must be used 
alongside another step for true 
‘sterility’ and to clear viruses
• Used in clean rooms, biological 
safety cabinets

pages.label: Slide 14
pages.text:
Ultraviolet (UV) irradiation sterilisation
• UV-C radiation (around 253nm 
wavelength) damage nucleic acids
and prevent microbial replication
• Effective against bacteria, fungi, viruses,
and bacterial spores (at higher ‘doses’)
• Very poor penetrative power… only 
works where the light directly reaches
• Still used on flat surfaces and where
shadows can be controlled

pages.label: Slide 15
pages.text:
Gamma irradiation sterilisation
• Sterilises by causing DNA strand breaks 
via ionising gamma ray radiation
• Usually uses the radioactive Cobalt-60 
isotope as the source of the radiation
• Commonly used to sterilise syringes, 
catheters, gloves, Pasteur pipettes, L-
shaped spreaders, most single-use 
plastics, that are already in their packages
• Can use Bacillus pumilus as a control
to check sterilisation occurs correctly

pages.label: Slide 16
pages.text:
Electron beam irradiation sterilisation
• High-energy electrons are used 
to cause fatal DNA damage in
microorganisms 
• Used to sweep a curtain of
high-energy electrons at
packaged medical devices
• No radioactive waste generated,
completes in minutes, very
low thermal impact

pages.label: Slide 17
pages.text:
X-ray sterilisation
• High-energy X-rays cause extensive,
fatal DNA damage in microorganisms
• Used in the generation of sterile
medical devices and pharmaceuticals
• X-rays are disorganised and can scatter
widely
• Provides excellent penetration into surfaces
• X-ray systems use 10 times as much energy 
compared to electron beam systems(!)

pages.label: Slide 18
pages.text: Electron Beam versus X-Ray Sterilisation

pages.label: Slide 19
pages.text:
Ethylene oxide (EtO) gas sterilisation
• Low-temperature gaseous process which 
exploits the alkylation of DNA and proteins to 
destroy microorganisms 
• Used to sterile catheters, 
endoscopes, electronics, and 
plastics
• Modern hospitals have these
machines in-house
• Bacillus subtilis can be used as a control
to check sterilisation occurs correctly

pages.label: Slide 20
pages.text:
Hydrogen peroxide vapour (VHP) sterilisation
• Uses vapourised hydrogen peroxide to
cause oxidative damage to microbe
cellular components
• Used to decontaminate an entire 
room/ward after an outbreak,
and sterilise medical devices
• Used by the NHS to destroy 
Clostridioides difficile spores, 
norovirus, MRSA, and other 
persistent pathogens

pages.label: Slide 21
pages.text:
Hydrogen peroxide gas plasma sterilisation
• Low-temperature plasma process
causes free-radical mediated
damage to microorganisms 
• Used to treat delicate, heat-sensitive or 
moisture sensitive surgical
instruments (endoscopes, etc.)
• Used extensively by the NHS for this
purpose

pages.label: Slide 22
pages.text:
Formaldehyde gas fumigation sterilisation
• A low-temperature gaseous process
• Formaldehyde acts as a very strong 
alkylating agent, causing cross-links to 
form between DNA, proteins, nucleic acids
• Historical extensive use in ‘formaldehyde 
bombs’ to sterilise hospital wards
• Extremely controversial at the moment,
NHS staff may have been exposed
above long-term safety limits… new regulations pending 2027

pages.label: Slide 23
pages.text:
Think of the reasons that this method is being
phased out…

pages.label: Slide 24
pages.text:
Peracetic acid sterilisation
• Peracetic acid is a liquid chemical
sterilant
• Causes extensive oxidation of 
proteins and membranes of 
microorganisms
• Used to sterilise flexible 
endoscopes (like those used in 
colonoscopies), and other
heat-sensitive equipment

pages.label: Slide 25
pages.text:
Ozone sterilisation
• Oxidative gaseous sterilant
• Causes the oxidation of 
cellular components of the 
microbes
• Also used as a specialist
method for the sterilisation
of medical devices

pages.label: Slide 26
pages.text:
Ultra-High Temperature (UHT) sterilisation
• 135-150°C for 2 to 5 seconds(!)
• Causes the thermal destruction of
microorganisms, leading to the 
commercial definition of ‘sterility’
• Used on shelf-stable milk, 
beverages, and ready-to-consume 
infant milk

pages.label: Slide 27
pages.text:
Food retort sterilisation
• Essentially a ‘specialised’ autoclave…
• Designed to process packaged foods
(canned soup, cans of veg., ready meals)
• Achieve ‘commercial sterility’ – meaning 
that no microorganisms that are capable 
of growing under the intended storage 
conditions can survive
• Concerned with food safety and shelf
stability rather than absolute sterility as we define it clinically

pages.text:
Please keep yourself safe if you work
with sterilisation techniques in the future!
Ensure that your employer and yourself are compliant with:
• Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974
• Control of Substances Hazardous to Health Regulations (COSHH)
• Pressure Systems Safety Regulations 2000 (PSSR)
• HSE Safety Requirements for Autoclaves (PM73)

• Ionising Radiations Regulations 2017 (IRR17)

Assessments
The same technologies that kill microorganisms can 
also very easily kill you too!

Summary
•
True sterilisation is: ‘the complete destruction or removal of 
viable microorganisms, including highly resistant forms 
such as bacterial endospores’. This differs to ‘disinfection’

applications

that achieve the required level of sterility assurance

Energy Metabolism in the Human Body 
Refers to the sum of all biochemical processes involved in the breakdown, 
utilization, and synthesis of energy-providing substrates throughout the entire 
body. These substrates primarily include carbohydrates, fats and proteins.
The process encompasses:
• Catabolism: The breakdown of complex molecules into simpler forms, 
releasing energy.
• Anabolism: The building up of compounds, which requires energy.
• Energy production: The conversion of nutrients into usable cellular energy, 
primarily in the form of ATP.
• Substrate interconversion: The transformation of one type of substrate into 
another, such as gluconeogenesis (eg protein to glucose) or lipogenesis (eg 
carbohydrate to fat).

Background: Breast cancer  
 
Breast cancer is the most commonly diagnosed cancer among females in the UK, 
accounting for approximately 15% of all new cancer cases in women (Cancer 
Research UK, 2023). While it is predominantly a disease affecting women, breast 
cancer can also occur in men, though it remains rare. Around 370 men in the UK 
are diagnosed with breast cancer annually, with approximately 80 deaths attributed 
to the disease each year (CRUK, 2023). 
 
A variety of risk factors have been associated with the development of breast 
cancer. These include ionising radiation exposure, atypical hyperplasia, family 
history, genetic mutations (e.g. BRCA1/2), and prolonged exposure to 
unopposed oestrogens (estrogen that is not balance by progesterone; ACS, 2023; 
Colditz & Bohlke, 2014). These factors can lead to genetic and epigenetic alterations 
in breast epithelial cells, promoting abnormal proliferation and tumourigenesis. A 
summary of key risk factors is provided in Table 1.

Breast cancer is broadly categorised into two main groups based on the presence or 
absence of invasion beyond the basement membrane (WHO Classification, 2019): 
 
A. Non-invasive (in situ) Carcinomas

pages.label: Page 3
pages.text:
3 
 
These lesions are confined to the ducts or lobules and do not penetrate the 
basement membrane into surrounding stroma. 
• 
Ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) 
• 
Lobular carcinoma in situ (LCIS) 
Although non-invasive, these lesions carry varying degrees of risk for progression to 
invasive cancer, especially DCIS. 
 
B. Invasive (Infiltrating) Carcinomas 
Invasive carcinomas are defined by malignant epithelial cells breaching the 
basement membrane and infiltrating the adjacent stromal tissue. Based on their 
histological characteristics, invasive breast carcinomas are further classified into 
subtypes, including: 
• 
Invasive ductal carcinoma (no special type, NST); most common (~70–
80%) 
• 
Invasive lobular carcinoma 
• 
Mucinous (colloid) carcinoma 
• 
Tubular carcinoma 
• 
Medullary carcinoma 
• 
Papillary carcinoma 
Each subtype has distinct morphological and clinical features, with tumour size, 
histological grade, nodal involvement, and molecular profile serving as key 
prognostic and treatment-determining factors (Rakha & Ellis, 2011). 
 
Molecular Classification and Biomarkers 
 
Advances in immunohistochemistry and molecular profiling have allowed further 
classification of breast cancer into subtypes based on receptor status: 
1. Hormone receptor-positive (ER and/or PR positive) 
2. HER2-positive 
(Human 
Epidermal 
Growth 
Factor 
Receptor 
2 
overexpression) 
3. Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC), negative for ER, PR, and HER2 
 
These molecular subtypes are not only prognostic but also guide therapeutic 
decisions. For example, hormone receptor-positive cancers may respond to 
endocrine therapy (e.g., tamoxifen or aromatase inhibitors), while HER2-positive 
tumours are amenable to targeted therapies such as trastuzumab (Perou et al., 
2000; Prat et al., 2015; Roy et al., 2023).

Breast Cancer Histopathology – revision notes 
 
1. Ductal Carcinoma In Situ (DCIS) 
• 
DCIS is non-invasive, confined within ducts; no basement membrane 
invasion. 
• 
Common architectural patterns: 
- 
Comedo: central necrosis, high grade, calcifications 
- 
Cribriform: punched-out spaces in epithelial sheets 
- 
Papillary: fibrovascular cores 
- 
Micropapillary: tufts of cells without fibrovascular cores 
- 
Solid: ducts fully filled with tumour cells 
• 
Grading based on nuclear pleomorphism, mitoses, and necrosis. 
• 
Myoepithelial cell layer is preserved – helps distinguish from invasive 
cancer. 
• 
Often detected via mammographic microcalcifications. 
2. Lobular Carcinoma In Situ (LCIS) 
• 
LCIS is a risk marker and non-obligate precursor to invasive cancer. 
• 
Usually an incidental finding; rarely presents with mass or calcification. 
• 
Histology: small, uniform, dyscohesive cells filling lobules. 
• 
Basement membrane intact – no invasion. 
• 
Loss of E-cadherin on immunohistochemistry. 
• 
Often ER/PR positive; HER2 negative. 
• 
Hormonal therapy may be considered to reduce future cancer risk. 
3. Invasive Ductal Carcinoma (IDC) 
• 
Most common invasive breast cancer (~70–80%). 
• 
H&E shows irregular nests or cords of tumour cells in desmoplastic 
stroma. 
• 
Retains E-cadherin expression. 
• 
May be associated with adjacent DCIS. 
• 
Typically forms glands; often shows necrosis and pleomorphism.

pages.label: Page 7
pages.text:
7 
 
• 
Presents as a palpable mass, usually visible on mammogram or 
ultrasound. 
4. Invasive Lobular Carcinoma (ILC) 
• 
Second most common invasive type. 
• 
Cells are dyscohesive due to loss of E-cadherin. 
• 
Classic pattern: single-file (Indian file) infiltration. 
• 
May show targetoid arrangement around ducts/lobules. 
• 
Often bilateral and multifocal. 
• 
Difficult to detect on mammography – MRI more sensitive. 
• 
Usually ER/PR-positive, HER2-negative (Luminal A subtype common). 
5. H&E Staining – Diagnostic Use 
• 
H&E is essential for assessing: 
- 
Architecture (ductal vs lobular) 
- 
Cytological features (pleomorphism, mitoses) 
- 
Stromal invasion vs in situ patterns 
- 
Tumour grade, necrosis, and inflammation 
• 
Cannot determine receptor status – IHC needed for ER, PR, HER2, Ki-67. 
6. Immunohistochemistry (IHC) Markers 
• 
E-cadherin: Present in IDC; Absent in ILC/LCIS 
• 
ER/PR: Hormonal status 
• 
HER2: Receptor overexpression, target for trastuzumab 
• 
Ki-67: Proliferation index, used to distinguish Luminal A vs B 
• 
Myoepithelial markers (p63, SMA, calponin): help confirm in situ lesions 
7. Molecular Subtypes of Breast Cancer 
• 
Luminal A: ER+, PR+, HER2–, low Ki-67 → good prognosis, hormonal 
therapy 
• 
Luminal B: ER+, PR±, HER2±, high Ki-67 → more aggressive 
• 
HER2-enriched: ER–, PR–, HER2+ → targeted therapy 
• 
Triple-negative (Basal-like): ER–, PR–, HER2– → poor prognosis, chemo-
sensitive

1. Ductal Carcinoma In Situ (DCIS)

DCIS is non-invasive, confined within ducts; no basement membrane invasion.

Common architectural patterns:

   - Comedo: central necrosis, high grade, calcifications

   - Cribriform: punched-out spaces in epithelial sheets

   - Papillary: fibrovascular cores

   - Micropapillary: tufts of cells without fibrovascular cores

   - Solid: ducts fully filled with tumour cells

Grading based on nuclear pleomorphism, mitoses, and necrosis.

Myoepithelial cell layer is preserved – helps distinguish from invasive cancer.

Often detected via mammographic microcalcifications.
2. Lobular Carcinoma In Situ (LCIS)

LCIS is a risk marker and non-obligate precursor to invasive cancer.

Usually an incidental finding; rarely presents with mass or calcification.

Histology: small, uniform, dyscohesive cells filling lobules.

Basement membrane intact – no invasion.

Loss of E-cadherin on immunohistochemistry.

Often ER/PR positive; HER2 negative.

Hormonal therapy may be considered to reduce future cancer risk.
3. Invasive Ductal Carcinoma (IDC)

Most common invasive breast cancer (~70–80%).

H&E shows irregular nests or cords of tumour cells in desmoplastic stroma.

Retains E-cadherin expression.

May be associated with adjacent DCIS.

Typically forms glands; often shows necrosis and pleomorphism.

Presents as a palpable mass, usually visible on mammogram or ultrasound.
4. Invasive Lobular Carcinoma (ILC)

Second most common invasive type.


Cells are dyscohesive due to loss of E-cadherin.

Classic pattern: single-file (Indian file) infiltration.

May show targetoid arrangement around ducts/lobules.

Often bilateral and multifocal.

Difficult to detect on mammography – MRI more sensitive.


5. H&E Staining – Diagnostic Use

H&E is essential for assessing:

   - Architecture (ductal vs lobular)

   - Cytological features (pleomorphism, mitoses)

   - Stromal invasion vs in situ patterns

   - Tumour grade, necrosis, and inflammation

Cannot determine receptor status – IHC needed for ER, PR, HER2, Ki-67.
6. Immunohistochemistry (IHC) Markers

E-cadherin: Present in IDC; Absent in ILC/LCIS

ER/PR: Hormonal status

HER2: Receptor overexpression, target for trastuzumab

Ki-67: Proliferation index, used to distinguish Luminal A vs B

Myoepithelial markers (p63, SMA, calponin): help confirm in situ lesions
7. Molecular Subtypes of Breast Cancer

Luminal A: ER+, PR+, HER2–, low Ki-67 → good prognosis, hormonal therapy

Luminal B: ER+, PR±, HER2±, high Ki-67 → more aggressive

HER2-enriched: ER–, PR–, HER2+ → targeted therapy

Triple-negative (Basal-like): ER–, PR–, HER2– → poor prognosis, chemo-sensitive

STUDENT SAFETY REGULATIONS.
The techniques used in microbiology are designed both to prevent unwanted micro-
organisms from the environment contaminating experimental cultures and to prevent 
laboratory cultures from "escaping" with the consequent danger of disease or pollution.
1. Regard EVERY microorganism as pathogenic, even if its identity is unknown. 
It could be a recognised pathogen.

glasses when in the laboratory. The lab coat should never be worn outside the 
laboratory.

laboratories.

must be left in the lockers and never bought into the laboratory.
7. Cover any cuts on your skin with a waterproof dressing prior to the lab 
session.
