Neoplasia Lecture 1 - Outline
General Introduction, Epidemiology & Classification of Cancer:
The following notes are provided as an aids memoir to the lecture and should not be regarded 
as a replacement to a textbook in any sense. Students are strongly encouraged to do additional 
reading from one of the recommended textbooks plus a few recent scientific articles.
Incidence of cancer, 22% of deaths due to cancer, second largest killer and the most feared 
disease in the western world. Cancer is characterised by uncontrolled cell division.  Normal 
cell division (which takes place in the embryo or in the skin, GIT and blood cells of an adult) 
versus cell division in cancer.  Functional steady state in the former - unregulated cell division 
in cancer. Other important differences include growth factor independency, loss of contact 
inhibition, loss of anchorage dependence, loss of adhesiveness, loss of density-dependent 
inhibition of growth, loss of differentiation & loss of normal relationship between cancer and 
neighbouring cells. Cancer is not a single disease but a family of hundred different diseases. 
Different types of cancer are treated differently and have different clinical outcomes. Common 
types of cancer in men (lung, colorectal, stomach and prostate) and women (breast, lung, 
cervix and colorectal). Leukaemias, lymphomas, cancer of brain, bone and kidney are more 
common in children.
Classification of cancer is based on two criteria (a) its biological behaviour and (b) type of cell 
or tissue from which it arises. If a cancer is aggressive i.e. it destroys surrounding tissues then 
it is called Malignant. Those tumours which do not invade other cells or tissues are called 
Benign. Benign neoplasms are generally slow-growing and relatively well-differentiated. 
Malignant neoplasms show rapid growth and poor differentiation. Both benign and malignant 
neoplasms can occur in epithelium, connective tissue and muscle and are classified further as 
follows. Benign tumour of lining epithelium is called papilloma - further sub-classified into 
squamous, columnar or transitional papillomas. Benign tumour of glandular epithelium is 
known as adenoma.  Benign tumours of connective tissue and muscle - use the name of the 
tissue followed by the suffix “oma”.  For example, lipoma (adipose tissue), fibroma (fibrous 
tissue), osteoma (bone) and myoma (muscle). Malignant neoplasms of the lining epithelium 
are carcinomas - further sub-classified into squamous, columnar or transitional carcinomas. 
Glandular epithelium -adenocarcinoma.  90% of all human malignancies are carcinomas – 
WHY???
Malignant neoplasms of bone, cartilage and muscle are sarcomas, whereas those of blood and 
lymphoid organs are leukaemias and lymphomas respectively.  Incidence of sarcomas around 
2%; leukaemias and lymphomas around 8%.
Some exceptions to the above nomenclature:  1) Melanoma - malignant tumour.
2)  Leukaemias and lymphomas are malignant cancers.
3) Blastomas is a suffix which is used to describe cancer which resemble embryonic tissue, for 
example, retinoblastoma is a childhood eye cancer and 
4) Some tumours are named after their discoverers, such as Hodgkin’s disease (lymphomas) 
and Wilm’s tumour (a childhood kidney cancer).

Invasion & Metastasis
Malignant neoplasms can spread in one of the following ways. 
Direct spread i.e. cancer spreading to the adjacent tissues. Tumour spread usually occurs 
along the path of least resistance which gives it a crab like appearance.
Vascular spread, generally, carcinomas (breast carcinoma, melanoma) spread via lymph 
vessels and sarcomas (osteosarcoma) spread through blood vessels. 
Transcoelomic spread - Spread of a malignant neoplasm in a body cavity such as pleural or 
peritoneal cavity.  For example, stomach or colon cancer can perforate the gut wall and 
spread through the peritoneal cavity to ovaries.
STEPS INVOLVED IN CANCER SPREAD 
1. Cell detachment - Malignant cells detach from the primary tumour because they lack 
the cell to cell adhesiveness.  Factors responsible for reduced cell adhesion are (i) 
absence or deficiency of inter-cellular junctional complexes (ii) absence or deficiency 
of adhesiveproteins, such as E-Cadherin or fibronectin. 
2. Destruction of basement membrane & CT matrix, malignant cells secrete various 
proteolytic enzymes (e.g. collagenases, gelatinases & stromelysins) to destroy the 
basement membrane and/or CT matrix around them. 
3. Invasion of vessel - cancer cells enter blood or lymph vessels by destroying vascular 
basement membrane. 
4. Migration,  tumour cells travel to other organs. For example, colo-rectal cancer 
spreading to the liver or lung cancer cells traveling via blood vessels to the brain.
5. Extravasation – coming out of the vessel when neoplastic cells reach a suitable site. 
6. Survival – at the new site against the body defences. 
7. Secondary tumour  - Multiplication and growth at the new site to form secondaries 
which are detached from the primary tumour.
Clinical Staging of Cancer 
The degree to which a cancer has spread at the time of diagnosis and its prognosis is 
described by CLINICAL STAGING. Note that clinical staging is different from the 
classification of cancer, which was covered in Lecture 1.
TNM system of clinical staging is preferred to other staging systems because it is used 
internationally and avoids confusion.
T denotes condition of the primary tumour.  Tis or T0 (T zero) is cancer which is confined to 
one site (carcinoma in situ), T1 through to T4 indicate increasing size of the primary tumour 
and its spread through the neighbouring tissues.
N stands for the extent of lymph node involvement.  N0 (N zero) means lymph nodes are free 
of cancer.  N1, N2 and N3 mean increasing extent of lymph node involvement.

Palindromic sequence

pages.label: Slide 31

C R I S P R / C A S  9
Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats

pages.label: Slide 32
pages.text:
Bacterial immunity
1. The bacterium acquires a segment of the foreign DNA
2. It inserts this DNA between two palindromic repeats at the CRISPR locus
3. The transcript from this locus is spliced so that each foreign DNA segment is 
paired with a palindromic repeat (which folds into a hairpin)
4. The processed RNA transcript pairs with a cas9 protein (an RNA-protein 
complex)
5. The RNA-protein complex scans foreign DNA for sequence matches
6. Matching sequence triggers splicing by cas9
7. The CRISPR locus is inherited by daughter bacteria (an ‘immunization’ card)

Cas9 interacts with a single stranded RNA 
molecule (a “guide” RNA or gRNA)
It cuts any sequence that matches its guide 
RNA
What if we replace the guide RNA with an RNA 
of our own construction (that matches human 
genome sequence)?

Effective at destroying harmful mutations

division
However, if we provide our own

S U M M A R Y
Gene therapy broadly consists of five steps, but each of these requires 
many challenging considerations
Traditional gene therapy attempts to insert therapeutic genetic 
material into host cells, but this can be short-lived and imprecise
Gene editing leverages the CRISPR/Cas9 system to precisely edit the 
genome, which has dramatic implications
All forms of gene therapy continue to improve, but there remain many 
ethical concerns
